title: Taught to the sun, told again
hook: the sun, a king, his son, and a teaching handed down until it was lost
carry: whenever dharma declines, god comes again

segments.voice: Yesterday, karma as lokasangraha: King Janaka reaching perfection through action, and Krishna working to lokasangraha: act to hold the world together.
screen: `KARMA.` · `LOKASANGRAHA: ACT TO HOLD THE WORLD TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: The sun. Manu. Ikshvaku. Three names at the start of chapter four, and they're a chain. Krishna says he taught this yoga, the yoga of action, to Vivasvan, the sun. Vivasvan told it to Manu. Manu told it to his son Ikshvaku. And so it was handed on, from one royal sage to the next. Then, over a long stretch of time, Krishna says, it was lost. That's why he's telling it again, now, to Arjuna, on a battlefield.
screen: `THE SUN, MANU, IKSHVAKU.` → `HANDED ON, KING TO KING.` → `LOST, AND TOLD AGAIN.`

segments.voice: The Gita's word for this handing on is parampara: one after another, teacher to student. And Krishna tells Arjuna why it's coming to him: because you are my devotee and my friend, and this is a deep secret. Arjuna, being Arjuna, hears a problem. Your birth was recent, he says. The sun's was long ago. How could you have taught him? Krishna's answer is the turn of the chapter. Many births have passed, for me and for you. I know them all. You don't. Then he describes his own coming. Though unborn, and Lord of all beings, he comes into being through his own power, his own maya. And he says when: whenever dharma declines and its opposite rises, he sends himself forth, age after age, to protect the good and set dharma back on its feet. This is the teaching behind every avatar story Hindus tell, Rama, Krishna, the fish, the man-lion. The word avatara, a coming down, isn't in these verses, but these are the verses people quote for it. And here's the link to our word. In the next verse, Krishna calls his birth and his action, his karma, divine. Whoever truly knows them isn't born again on leaving the body, but comes to him. So the one teaching the yoga of action is also acting: taking birth, entering the world, doing the work. The commentators read his coming differently. Shankara speaks of the Lord appearing to take a body by his own maya, while remaining unborn. Ramanuja insists the Lord's births are real, taken freely by his own will, not forced on him by karma, as ours are.
screen: `PARAMPARA: ONE AFTER ANOTHER.` · `MANY BIRTHS: I KNOW THEM, YOU DON'T.` · `AVATARA: THE COMING DOWN.` · `HIS BIRTH AND KARMA ARE DIVINE.` · then, large: `WHENEVER DHARMA DECLINES, I COME.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing someone taught you, a recipe, a prayer, a knot, how to apologize, and picture the person who taught you, then, if you can, the person who taught them. Let the chain run back as far as you can see, into people you'll never know, and sit with the whole line behind one small skill. If you pray, you can give thanks for the whole chain.
Karma. In chapter four, a yoga of action handed down teacher to student, lost, and told again by one whose own birth and action are divine.
Your line: whenever dharma declines, God comes again. Tomorrow, a verse some families say before eating. Until then.

howItsDone: In Hindu teaching lineages, a teaching is received from a teacher in an unbroken parampara, and Gita 4.7–8, 'whenever dharma declines', is a verse some Hindus learn by heart.

Vivasvan.meaning: the sun, first to receive the yoga of action

Manu.meaning: the sun's student, who passed the teaching to his son

Ikshvaku.meaning: Manu's son, a royal sage in the teaching's chain

parampara.meaning: one after another: teaching handed from teacher to student

maya.meaning: the Lord's own power, by which he takes birth

Ramanuja.meaning: a great Vaishnava teacher who wrote a Gita commentary

avatara.meaning: a coming down: God taking a form in the world

sources.ref: Bhagavad Gita 4.1–4.3 (Vivasvan, Manu, Ikshvaku; parampara; the teaching lost and told again)
Bhagavad Gita 4.4–4.9 (Arjuna's objection; many births; 'by my own maya'; whenever dharma declines; divine birth and action)

notes: Shankara on 4.6: the Lord, by his own maya, appears to be born and embodied; Ramanuja on 4.5–6: the Lord's births are real, by his own will (atma-sankalpa), and his body is not made of karma-bound matter. Both compressed; confirm fairness.
Editor pass: 'both would agree on the shape of the chapter' (an unsourced claim about Shankara and Ramanuja) became 'the shape of the chapter holds either way'.
4.3 'my devotee and my friend' and 'this is a supreme secret': confirm paraphrase.
This day avoids 'avatar' in the voice, since the Gita here uses verbs of coming into being and sending forth; the trapdoor names it as the common term.
